title: Tanisha D.
text:
I am looking at the NHL data. This data is slightly more complicated than the pwhl data, because there is no empty_net column or a goalie_change event. Instead, there is a 4-digit Situation Code, structured like this: [Away Goalie][Away skaters][Home skaters][Home Goalie]. If either the first or the last characters are 0, then there is an empty net (the code may look like 1560, 0651, 0440, 0551, 1550, etc.). We also have to make sure the goalie pull is in the last 5 minutes of the period, just to make sure we are not accidentially counting a goalie change. For all of these instances where there is an empty net, we can record the score, and then map whether the team that pulled their goalie (the team that is losing) ended up tying or winning the game.


Code
#Load the libraries
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(hms)
library(stringr)
library(scales)




Code
#Read in the NHL data
nhl = read_csv("../data/raw/hockey_data/nhl_games_2024_2026.csv")



Cleaning and Wrangling the data


Code
#Find all events
events <- nhl %>%
  arrange(game_id, sortOrder) %>%
  group_by(game_id) %>%
  fill(
    details.awayScore,
    details.homeScore,
    .direction = "down"
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

#Find all goalie pulls 
events <- events %>%
  mutate(
    situationId = as.character(situationCode),
    away_goalie = str_sub(situationCode, 1, 1),
    home_goalie = str_sub(situationCode, 4, 4)
  ) %>%
  group_by(game_id) %>%
  arrange(sortOrder, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    prev_away_goalie = lag(away_goalie),
    prev_home_goalie = lag(home_goalie)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

#Find all away goalie pulls
away_pulls <- events %>%
  filter(
    prev_away_goalie == "1",
    away_goalie == "0",
    periodDescriptor.number == 3,
    timeInPeriod >= hms::as_hms("00:15:00")
  ) %>%
  transmute(
    game_id,
    team = "Away",
    situationCode,
    score_at_pull = details.awayScore,
    opponent_score_at_pull = details.homeScore,
    periodDescriptor.number,
    timeInPeriod,
    sortOrder
  )

#Find all home goalie pulls
home_pulls <- events %>%
  filter(
    prev_home_goalie == "1",
    home_goalie == "0",
    periodDescriptor.number == 3,
    timeInPeriod >= hms::as_hms("00:15:00")
  ) %>%
  transmute(
    game_id,
    team = "Home",
    situationCode,
    score_at_pull = details.homeScore,
    opponent_score_at_pull = details.awayScore,
    periodDescriptor.number,
    timeInPeriod,
    sortOrder
  )




Code
#Combine home and away pulls
pulls_5min <- bind_rows(away_pulls, home_pulls) %>%
  filter(score_at_pull < opponent_score_at_pull) %>%
  arrange(game_id, team, sortOrder) %>%
  group_by(game_id, team) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  ungroup()




Code
#Find the final score for all the games in the last three years
final_scores <- events %>%
  group_by(game_id) %>%
  summarise(
    away_final = max(details.awayScore, na.rm = TRUE),
    home_final = max(details.homeScore, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )




Code
#Merge the results back onto the pulls 
results_5min <- pulls_5min %>%
  select(-any_of(c(
    "away_final", "home_final",
    "final_team_score", "final_opponent_score",
    "outcome", "seconds_remaining", "minutes_remaining"
  ))) %>%
  left_join(final_scores, by = "game_id") %>%
  mutate(
    final_team_score = if_else(
      team == "Away", away_final, home_final
    ),

    final_opponent_score = if_else(
      team == "Away", home_final, away_final
    ),

    seconds_remaining = 1200 - as.numeric(timeInPeriod),
    minutes_remaining = seconds_remaining / 60,

    outcome = case_when(
      is.na(final_team_score) ~ NA_character_,
      final_team_score > final_opponent_score ~ "Win",
      final_team_score == final_opponent_score ~ "Tie",
      TRUE ~ "Loss"
    )
  )




Exploratory Data Analysis and Visualization


Code
overall_results <- results_5min %>%
  summarise(
    attempts = n(),
    wins = sum(outcome == "Win"),
    ties = sum(outcome == "Tie"),
    losses = sum(outcome == "Loss"),
    win_pct = wins / attempts * 100,
    tie_or_win_pct = (wins + ties) / attempts * 100
  )

results_5min %>%
  count(outcome) %>%
  mutate(
    outcome = factor(
      outcome,
      levels = c("Win", "Tie", "Loss")

  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = outcome, y = n, fill = outcome)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +

    aes(label = paste0(n, " (", round(n/sum(n)*100, 1), "%)")),
    vjust = -0.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Outcome of Pulling the Goalie",
    subtitle = "Teams trailing in the final five minutes",
    x = "Final outcome",
    y = "Number of games"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +

results_5min <- results_5min%>%
  mutate(score_deficit = opponent_score_at_pull - score_at_pull)

title: Feride K
text:
Visualization 1: When are goalies pulled?

This visualization shows how many candidate goalie pulls happen at different times in the third period.



Code
# Filter third-period goalie pulls
pull_timing <- pulls %>%
  filter(
    period == 3,
    !is.na(pull_time_remaining_sec),
    between(pull_time_remaining_sec, 0, 600)
  ) %>%
  mutate(minutes_remaining = pull_time_remaining_sec / 60)

ggplot(pull_timing, aes(x = minutes_remaining)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 1,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  labs(
    title = "When Do Teams Pull Their Goalies?",
    subtitle = "PWHL candidate goalie pulls in the final 10 minutes",
    x = "Minutes remaining in the third period",
    y = "Number of goalie pulls"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Appendix B — Case Study: Women’s Pockets
text:
This is the report we looked at: https://pudding.cool/2018/08/pockets/
A quick summary: this article looks at how womens’ pockets are smaller than mens’. It does this by looking at multiple womens’ and mens’ jeans to see the size differences between the two, and then points out which specific jeans can hold different everyday items (phones, a pen, a wallet, etc.).
Comments about data story: - The introduction with visualizations evolves as the reader scrolls from the why the women’s pockets are generally smaller than men to comparing the sizes for the front,back and side pockets for both genders. -They also mention the idea behind why women’s pockets are small from history. - It becomes interactive after the introduction, so that readers could potentially find their own pair of jeans and see how it compares to the rest. It also lets the reader choose their descriptive statistic (average, smallest, largest) to see how pockets work for different fits (skinny vs. straight). The interactive website makes the story unravel in a unique and engaging way. I enjoyed the comparisons and ability to set the parameters yourself. From shapes, styles, prices and brands the article gives us a sense of the evolution of pockets and why the reader should care. - The story unfolds in a very casual manner (eg. “So real”) bringing a sort of relatability. They have identified the a problem in the society that affects around 50% of the global population, women.
